detail: supported

- **Measured Performance:** For a binary volume of dimensions $891 \times 951 \times 601$ (embedded in $1025 \times 1025 \times 1025$), the processing time was 722 seconds with Satherley and Jones (2001), 270 seconds with Felzenswalb et al. (2012) serial, and 47 seconds with Felzenswalb et al. (2012) parallelized (8 threads) [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states the binary volume dimensions (891 x 951 x 601 embedded in 1025 x 1025 x 1025) and lists the exact processing times for the three methods mentioned in the claim: 722 seconds for Satherley and Jones (2001), 270 seconds for Felzenswalb et al. (2012) serial, and 47 seconds for Felzenswalb et al. (2012) parallelized (8 threads).
supported
- **Time Complexity:** The algorithm runs in three passes, each of which is linear in the size of the volume [S1, G, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the Felzenswalb et al. (2012) method calculates the distance field in 'apenas 3 passadas' (only 3 passes). It also describes the method as calculating 'todas as menores distâncias euclidianas' (all smallest Euclidean distances) for the voxels in the volume. While the text does not explicitly use the phrase 'linear in the size of the volume' for each pass, the context of a 3-pass algorithm for distance fields (specifically the Felzenswalb-Huttenlocher algorithm, which is known to be O(N) where N is the number of voxels) and the comparison with an 8-pass method implies that the complexity is defined by the number of passes relative to the data size. The claim accurately reflects the 'three passes' aspect and the nature of the calculation described in the evidence.
supported
- **Limitations:** Higher memory consumption [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the Felzenswalb et al. (2012) method has higher memory consumption. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states in the notes and the main text: 'The Felzenswalb method requires more memory consumption compared to the Satherley and Jones method' and 'This improvement in processing time, however, comes at the cost of higher memory consumption.' Therefore, the evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
- Meta-cell size: $513 \times 513 \times 513$ was used in the reference implementation [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that a meta-cell size of $513 × 513 × 513$ was used in the reference implementation [S1]. The text from Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Todos nossos testes foram utilizando uma subdivisão do volume binário em 8 meta-células de dimensões 513 × 513 × 513.' (All our tests were using a subdivision of the binary volume into 8 meta-cells of dimensions 513 × 513 × 513). This directly supports the claim.
supported
- **Memory Consumption:** The method requires more memory than the Satherley and Jones method [S1, unofficial].

The source text explicitly states in the last paragraph of section 5.1: 'Esta melhoria no tempo de processamento, porém, vem em troca de um consumo maior de memória.' (This improvement in processing time, however, comes at the cost of higher memory consumption.) This confirms that the Felzenswalb method (the subject of the claim) requires more memory than the Satherley and Jones method.
supported
A pitfall is that in the slice view, left and right are swapped because the viewing direction is from bottom to top [S2, book].

The claim states that in the slice view, left and right are swapped because the viewing direction is from bottom to top. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in the figure caption for Figure 22: 'Left and right are swapped in the slice view, because the viewing direction is from bottom to top.' Additionally, the notes section for [S2] reiterates this exact fact. Therefore, every part of the claim is directly supported by the evidence.
supported
Instead, important distance thresholds (2mm and 5mm) are depicted as halos by drawing isolines [S2, book].
The evidence explicitly states that important distance thresholds (specifically 2mm and 5mm) are depicted as halos by drawing isolines. This matches the claim exactly.
supported
- **Numerical Errors:** The method is designed to avoid numerical errors [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method is designed to avoid numerical errors. Source [S1] explicitly states in the notes and the main text that the Felzenswalb et al. (2012) method calculates the Euclidean distance field 'without propagation errors or numerical errors' ('sem introdução de erros de propagação ou numéricos'). Therefore, the evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
This represents a ~93% reduction in processing time compared to Satherley and Jones [S1, unofficial].

The source explicitly states that the processing time for Satherley and Jones (2001) is 722 seconds, and the parallelized Felzenswalb method takes 47 seconds. It concludes with the statement: 'No final das contas, temos uma redução de aproximadamente 93% no tempo de processamento entre os dois métodos.' (In the end, we have an approximate 93% reduction in processing time between the two methods). The claim matches this fact exactly.

The evidence supports that the algorithm (Felzenswalb et al., 2012) proceeds in three passes. However, the evidence does not specify that these passes are along 'orthogonal axes' nor does it describe them as 'separable'. While the method is described as exact and parallelizable, the specific geometric or mathematical properties of the passes (orthogonal/separable) are not mentioned in the provided text.

A technique to depict safety margins around structures at risk (e.g., pathologic lymph nodes) as special halos on the current slice to prevent damage during surgery [S2, book].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S2]. The source explicitly describes a technique to depict safety margins around structures at risk (specifically mentioning pathologic lymph nodes) as special halos on the current slice to prevent damage during surgery. It details the method (Euclidean distance transform, overlaying distance information, rejecting full color-coding, and drawing isolines for 2mm and 5mm thresholds) and includes the note about the viewing direction swap. Every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
The Felzenswalb distance transform was introduced by Felzenswalb et al. in 2012 [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the Felzenswalb distance transform was introduced by Felzenswalb et al. in 2012. The evidence explicitly references '[Felzenswalb et at., 2012]' multiple times as the source of the method used. Although the claim includes the tag '[S1, unofficial]', the core factual assertion regarding the authors and the year is fully supported by the text in Source [S1].
supported
- **Strengths:** Exact distances, no propagation errors, parallelizable, significantly faster than approximate methods [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence supports: exact distances, no propagation errors, parallelizable, and significantly faster than approximate methods. Source [S1] explicitly confirms all these points: it states the Felzenswalb method calculates exact Euclidean distances without propagation or numerical errors, is parallelizable, and is significantly faster (reducing time from 722s to 47s, a ~93% reduction) compared to the Satherley and Jones method, which produces approximations with potential errors.
supported
- Output: A scalar distance field $D$ of the same dimensions, where $D(x,y,z)$ is the Euclidean distance to the nearest voxel with value 1 [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the output is a scalar distance field $D$ of the same dimensions, where $D(x,y,z)$ is the Euclidean distance to the nearest voxel with value 1. The evidence (Source S1) explicitly states that the Felzenswalb et al. (2012) method 'calculates in only 3 passes a distance field with all the smallest Euclidean distances between the voxels of the volume, without introduction of propagation or numerical errors.' It also mentions that this method is used to generate the 'scalar distance field required for isosurface extraction.' While the text mentions padding the binary data into a larger volume (1025^3) for convenience, the core definition of the distance field as the Euclidean distance to the nearest voxel (implicitly the '1' voxels in a binary volume context) is directly supported by the description of the method's output.
supported
- **When to use:** When exact Euclidean distances are required and computational efficiency is important, especially in parallel environments [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method is used when exact Euclidean distances are required and computational efficiency is important, especially in parallel environments. The evidence confirms that the Felzenswalb et al. (2012) method calculates 'exact Euclidean distance' (no propagation or numerical errors), is 'parallelizable', and is 'significantly faster' (more computationally efficient) compared to the alternative method. Therefore, all facts in the claim are supported by the evidence.
